voting_system.label: Ranked-choice voting
voting_system.primaryExplanation: Each party's primary uses ranked-choice voting whenever 3 or more candidates (or 2 candidates plus a declared write-in) qualify for that party's ballot — voters rank their choices rather than picking just one.
voting_system.primarySnippet: 21-A M.R.S. §1(27-C): "'Elections determined by ranked-choice voting' means any of the following elections in which 3 or more candidates have qualified to be listed on the ballot for a particular office or at least 2 such candidates plus one or more declared write-in candidates have qualified... (A) Primary elections for the offices of United States Senator, United States Representative to Congress..."
voting_system.generalExplanation: Voters rank candidates in order of preference. If no one has more than half of first-choice votes, the last-place candidate is eliminated and their voters' ballots move to their next choice, repeating until someone has a majority — Maine was the first state to use this for federal elections, in 2018.
voting_system.generalSnippet: 21-A M.R.S. §723-A(2): "If a candidate has been assigned ranking number one on more than 50% of all ballots cast for the particular office for which the candidate is running... that candidate is declared the winner... If no candidate has been assigned ranking number one on more than 50%... the ranked-choice voting count must proceed in rounds... the last-place candidate is removed from consideration and a new round begins."

bio_summary.value: Paul LePage knows what it is like to struggle. Born into a broken home, Paul’s father handed him a 50-cent coin and told him to tell the doctors he fell down the stairs as he laid battered in a Lewiston hospital. 11-year-old Paul LePage took that coin, and left the hospital. He never returned home. Homeless, finding work and a place to sleep day-to-day, it was a horse stable worker who told him, “If it is to be, it is up to me.” Paul took that phrase to heart, finished high school, earned a college and graduate degree, and went on to become one of New England’s most successful businesspeople, creating jobs and growing the economy.
